# Spam detection and SpamBrain

Google said spam is stopped at indexing: index selection loads most spam signals and keeps documents detected as spam out of the index, and Google's spam policies say violating sites may rank lower or not appear at all. Google has used statistical models against spam for over 20 years and now uses more and more AI; it said SpamBrain is built on Gemini and fine-tuned for spam, which is not in its documentation. Figures said on stage differ from the record: Google's 2021 webspam report gives 2018 as SpamBrain's launch year (2022 was mentioned on stage), and its 2022 report's '5 times more spam sites' compares 2022 with 2021, with 200 times more than at launch, rather than comparing SpamBrain with older algorithms. Google said its testing shows more than 99% of visits from Search are spam-free, a figure in its 2022 webspam report. Google said spam metadata such as white-on-white text is stored with a page's tokens (not in its docs), and its scaled content abuse policy covers automatically translated scraped content. Day 3 put the scale in numbers: Google discovers about 40 billion spammy pages a day, the figure in its webspam report for 2020 and its How Search Works page (a Day 3 slide headed 'In 2023' repeated it, and the quality talk said tens of billions), and its spam systems remove a very large amount before results are served. Google said AI has changed how it builds spam updates, letting it evaluate more candidates, catch new types of spam and launch faster; four spam updates had shipped in 2026 by 2 October, the September 2026 one still rolling out. Google repeated its aim of keeping more than 99% of results spam-free, which its webspam reports measure as visits from Search. Keyword stuffing remains a policy violation, and Google counts AI slop, mass-produced LLM content, as scaled content abuse that it is working hard to remove. Day 1's second recording added that the crawl scheduler very likely deprioritises URLs or sites known to be historically spammy. On Day 2 the non-Latin-script talk cited the October 2023 spam update, whose post says it improved coverage in many languages, naming Turkish, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Hindi and Chinese, particularly against cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam. Author's view: the post names neither Persian nor Arabic and does not mention link spam, so it does not show that the bought links the presenter saw working in those languages were addressed.

## What to do

- Remove leftover hidden text and keyword blocks; spam markers are stored with the page's tokens.
- Have machine translations reviewed and adapted by native speakers before publishing them at scale.
- When quoting SpamBrain figures, use the documented ones: launched in 2018, and 5 times more spam sites detected in 2022 than in 2021.
- Quote 40 billion spammy pages a day as Google's published figure (webspam report for 2020, How Search Works), not as a 2023 measurement.
- Do not treat keyword-density or word-count scores from CMS plug-ins as editorial targets.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to A/B testing says never to show one set of URLs to Googlebot and a different set to humans: that is cloaking, which is against Google's spam policies whether or not a test is running.

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Hidden text is recorded at token level: Google stores spam metadata such as white-on-white text with the tokens, so leftover hidden keyword blocks are a liability, not neutral clutter, and should be removed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C343` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-HTM-06`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.
  <br><sub>`D2-C612` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · Extends [D1-C048](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The October 2023 spam update cited in the non-Latin-script talk names neither Persian nor Arabic (only 'other languages') and lists cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam, not link spam, so it does not show that the bought links the presenter saw working in Persian or Arabic search were addressed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C979` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · [October 2023 Spam Update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/10/october-2023-spam-update), [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The SpamBrain launch year mentioned on stage, with hesitation, was 2022, which does not match Google's documented 2018; 2022 is the year of the improvements described in Google's 2022 webspam report, so cite 2018 as the launch year.
  <br><sub>`D2-C672` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The '5 times more spam sites' figure said on stage matches Google's 2022 webspam report, but the report compares 2022 with 2021 (and gives 200 times since launch), not SpamBrain with earlier algorithms; quote the documented comparison.
  <br><sub>`D2-C675` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.
  <br><sub>`D2-C692` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Do not treat keyword-density or word-count scores from CMS plugins as editorial targets: Google's spam policies treat filling a page with keywords to manipulate rankings as keyword stuffing, and Google says it has no preferred word count.
  <br><sub>`D3-C099` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The spoken 'tens of billions of spam pages' a day matches Google's How Search Works page, which says its systems find 40 billion spammy pages every day, and the later Day 3 slide '40B spammy pages detected every day' (under 'In 2023'); cite 40 billion a day.
  <br><sub>`D3-C200` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [Detecting spam to bring you relevant and reliable results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/detecting-spam/)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Cite 40 billion spammy pages a day as Google's published figure, from its webspam report for 2020 and its How Search Works page: the slide's 'In 2023' heading does not make it a 2023 measurement, because the 2021 and 2022 reports give no daily count.
  <br><sub>`D3-C241` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, What are quality updates · [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2020](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2021/04/how-we-fought-search-spam-2020), [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/04/webspam-report-2021), [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022), [Detecting spam to bring you relevant and reliable results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/detecting-spam/)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's webspam reports measure the 99% figure as visits from Search (2020 and 2022 reports) or searches (2021 report) that are spam-free, not as search results; cite it as more than 99% of visits from Search being spam-free.
  <br><sub>`D3-C276` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, What are quality updates · [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2020](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2021/04/how-we-fought-search-spam-2020), [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/04/webspam-report-2021), [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022)</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-HTM-06`: Never hide text from users, such as white-on-white or off-screen keyword blocks
- Requirement `DEV-INT-10`: Publish machine-translated language versions only after human review and localisation
- Requirement `DEV-PRF-01`: Keep connect time and time to first byte low and stable under crawler load
- Requirement `DEV-SPM-02`: Do not generate large sets of low-value pages from templates, feeds or LLM output
- Glossary term *AI slop*
- Glossary term *Scaled content abuse*
- Glossary term *Spam update*
- Glossary term *SpamBrain*
